232.title: What contemplation is
232.hook: a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus, being with God rather than thinking about him (CCC 2715)
232.carry: I look at him, he looks at me
232.howItsDone: Many Catholics practice silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament in Eucharistic adoration, sitting in a church or chapel simply to be with Christ, often for an hour at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the empty tomb, and camp four closed. Your line was he goes before you. Did you pause at the door of your ordinary place? Today camp five begins: the depths. And it begins with how to pray without words. Day two hundred thirty-two.

In the 1800s, in the little French village of Ars, the parish priest was a man named John Vianney, now a saint. People noticed an old farmer who would stop in the church every day and sit there for a long time, not moving his lips, not reading, not holding beads. Just sitting, looking toward the tabernacle. The priest finally asked him what he did all that time. And the farmer gave an answer so simple that the Catholic Church put it in its Catechism. Today's word is what he was doing.
screen: `A VILLAGE IN FRANCE, THE 1800S.` → `AN OLD FARMER, SITTING, LOOKING.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL THAT TIME?`

segments.voice: First, the farmer's answer. As the story is told, he said: I look at him, and he looks at me. That's it. No technique. No words. Two people looking at each other. The Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus, and it tells this story to explain it. Second, the word itself. Contemplation comes from Latin, and inside it is templum, the same root as temple. Originally a templum was a patch of sky or ground marked out by Roman priests for watching carefully. To contemplate was to mark out a space and look, with full attention. Catholics took the word and pointed it at God. Third, how it's different. Catholics describe three expressions of prayer. Vocal prayer uses words: the Our Father, the rosary. Meditation uses the mind: you think about a Gospel scene, you turn it over. Contemplation is simpler than both. It's being with God rather than thinking about him. Saint Teresa of Avila, a Spanish nun of the 1500s, described it as time spent alone with the one we know loves us, like close friends. You don't need to talk the whole time with a close friend. Fourth, the psalm we met back in camp four says it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be still and see that I am God." Be still. See. The Church teaches that contemplation isn't just for monks and nuns. It's a gift God can give anyone, in a kitchen or a car or a pew. And the farmer from Ars is the proof: no degree, no method. He just showed up, and looked.
screen: `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.` · `TEMPLUM: A SPACE MARKED OUT TO WATCH.` · `WORDS, THEN THOUGHT, THEN GAZE.` · `NOT ONLY FOR MONKS.` · then, large: `BE STILL AND SEE THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a crucifix or an icon for a minute, or longer. If you have one nearby, place it in front of you. If not, a picture on your phone, a candle, or simply the sky through a window. Settle and breathe. Don't try to think anything about it. Just look. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back to looking. If you pray, you can let yourself be looked at in return, the way the farmer did. If you don't, just rest in seeing one thing fully. The bell holds the time.
Contemplation. From the Latin templum, a space marked out for watching. A gaze of faith: being with God rather than thinking about him. Today's word.
Your line: I look at him, he looks at me. Today, once, stop and simply look at something for thirty seconds, without your phone and without a thought to finish. Day two hundred thirty-two.

contemplation means thinking hard about God

233.title: Lectio divina, 1: read
233.hook: the monks' ladder of four steps; first, read a short passage slowly
233.howItsDone: Many Catholics practice lectio divina with the day's Mass readings, alone or in parish groups, reading a short passage slowly several times before moving on to meditation, prayer and quiet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplation: the old farmer of Ars, who said I look at him, he looks at me. What did you look at for thirty seconds? Today, a ladder that climbs toward that gaze, one rung at a time. Day two hundred thirty-three.
screen: `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.`

segments.voice: Think about how you read most days. Scrolling. Skimming. Half a headline, a thumb flick, the next thing. By the end of the day you've read thousands of words and can't remember ten. Now picture a monastery in the Alps, about nine hundred years ago. A monk named Guigo, the prior of the Carthusians, writes a short letter to a friend about a different way to read. He describes it as a ladder with four rungs, reaching from the ground up to heaven. The first rung is today, and it's the simplest one: read. But slowly.
screen: `SCROLLING, SKIMMING, FORGETTING.` → `A MONK IN THE ALPS, 900 YEARS AGO.` → `A LADDER WITH FOUR RUNGS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Lectio divina is Latin for divine reading, or holy reading. Monks had practiced it for centuries before Guigo. Saint Benedict's Rule, from the 500s, sets aside hours of each day for it. Guigo's gift was to describe its steps. Second, the ladder. Guigo names four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation. Over the next four days we'll climb one a day. He sums them up, roughly: reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes. He was echoing Jesus's words in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." Third, what reading means here. Not reading a lot. Reading a little, slowly, more than once. A single verse, a few lines at most. In the ancient world, people usually read out loud, even alone, so monks would murmur the words under their breath. Reading was something your mouth and ears did too, not only your eyes. Guigo compares it to putting food in your mouth: you're not eating yet, but you've taken a bite. Fourth, how to choose. Catholics often take the day's Gospel from Mass, or a psalm. We'll carry one verse for all four rungs, so you can climb with it. Here it is, Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." That's the whole reading. It doesn't need more. Reading slowly is the opposite of scrolling: you're not looking for the next thing. You're staying with this one.
screen: `LECTIO DIVINA: HOLY READING.` · `READ, MEDITATE, PRAY, CONTEMPLATE.` · `A LITTLE, SLOWLY, OUT LOUD.` · `ONE VERSE FOR ALL FOUR RUNGS.` · then, large: `COME TO ME, ALL YOU THAT ARE BURDENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse three times. Settle and breathe. Here's the verse again: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Now say it yourself, quietly, under your breath, the way monks did. Slowly. Then a second time, even slower. Then a third time, and notice which word catches, the one that sticks out. Don't explain it yet. That's tomorrow. Just notice the word. Whether you pray or not, reading slowly is the whole job today. The bell holds the time.
Lectio divina. Latin for holy reading: a short passage, read slowly, the first rung of the monks' ladder. Today's word.
Your line: read slowly. Today, read one thing, a message, a paragraph, a label, twice as slowly as usual, and see what you catch. Day two hundred thirty-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy name for Bible study.
what it means: reading a few lines slowly, aloud, more than once, as the first step up a ladder of prayer.

234.title: Lectio divina, 2: meditate
234.hook: chew on one word the way a cow chews the cud
234.howItsDone: In Catholic tradition, meditation means reflecting on a passage of Scripture or a mystery of faith with mind, imagination and heart, often during the rosary or after the day's Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lectio divina, the first rung: read slowly. Your line was read slowly. And our verse: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Which word caught? Today, the second rung. Day two hundred thirty-four.

If you've ever driven past a field of cows, you've seen them lying there, jaws going, round and round, for what seems like hours. They're not eating anything new. They're chewing the cud: bringing back up what they already ate and chewing it again, so they can actually get the good out of it. It doesn't sound like a picture of prayer. But the medieval monks loved it. They said that after you read a word, you should chew on it like that. The second rung of the ladder is exactly this.
screen: `COWS IN A FIELD, CHEWING.` → `BRINGING IT BACK UP, AGAIN.` → `THE MONKS LOVED THIS PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Meditatio is Latin for meditation. In Catholic prayer, meditation doesn't mean emptying your mind. It means filling it with one thing and turning it over. The monks had another name for it, ruminatio, rumination, from the Latin for chewing the cud. Guigo, who described the ladder, says reading puts the food in your mouth, and meditation chews it and breaks it down. Second, the root it grows from. Back in camp four we prayed Psalm 1. In the Douay-Rheims, the blessed man is the one whose "will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word there, hagah, means to murmur, to mutter over something. Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey. Meditation is holding on to a word and not letting go. Third, the model. Catholics often point to Mary. After the shepherds came at Christmas, Luke says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't understand everything. She kept it, and kept turning it. Fourth, how it works with our verse. You take the one word that caught you yesterday, and you ask it questions. If it was burdened: what am I carrying? Since when? If it was come: come where? Come how? If it was refresh: what would that feel like? You're not studying the verse like a textbook. You're letting it meet your actual life. The Catechism says meditation engages thought, imagination, emotion and desire. Your whole self, chewing one small word.
screen: `MEDITATIO: CHEW IT OVER.` · `HAGAH: A LION GROWLING OVER PREY.` · `MARY KEPT THESE WORDS, PONDERING.` · `ASK YOUR WORD QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word from the verse. Settle and breathe. Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Pick one word. Come, or burdened, or refresh, or whichever one caught you. Now say it slowly, on your breath, again and again. Between repetitions, let it ask you a question about your own day. Don't hurry to an answer. Keep chewing. If you pray, you can do this in God's presence. The bell holds the time.
Meditatio. Latin for meditation: the second rung, chewing on one word from the reading, turning it over, letting it meet your life. Today's word.
Your line: chew the word. Today, bring your word back up three times, in line, at a red light, over the sink, and chew on it again. Day two hundred thirty-four.

original.note: Latin: meditation, the second rung of Guigo's ladder.

what it means: in Catholic prayer, chewing on one word of Scripture until it meets your life.

sources.ref: Guigo II, The Ladder of Monks (Scala claustralium)

235.title: Lectio divina, 3: pray
235.hook: answer God with what the word stirred up
235.howItsDone: In lectio divina Catholics move from reading and reflecting to speaking to God in their own words about what the passage stirred, and in the Mass the congregation answers each reading with a response.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meditatio, the second rung: chewing one word like a cow chews the cud. Your line was chew the word. What did your word ask you? Today, the third rung: you answer. Day two hundred thirty-five.

Imagine getting a long, careful letter from someone who loves you. You read it slowly. You read it again. You think about it all day. And then you never write back. Not a word. That would be strange. But it's what a lot of us do with Scripture: we read it, maybe think about it, and close the book. The monks said there's a third step, and it's the one that turns reading into a conversation. You answer. Today's word is the Latin for that answer.
screen: `A LETTER FROM SOMEONE WHO LOVES YOU.` → `AND YOU NEVER WRITE BACK.` → `THE THIRD STEP: ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Oratio is Latin for prayer, but also for a speech. It's related to the word for mouth. It's where English gets oration and oratory. It means speaking, out loud or inside, directly to someone. Second, the turn. Reading and meditation are about the word. Prayer is talking to the one who spoke it. Guigo says meditation makes the soul see what it lacks, and hunger for it, and then prayer asks. If yesterday your word was burdened, and you found you're carrying something heavy, today you tell God about it. Plainly. Third, the model. Catholics often point to the boy Samuel in the Temple. God calls his name in the night, three times, and he keeps running to the old priest Eli. Finally Eli tells him how to answer, and Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." That's the posture: God speaks first, and prayer is the reply. Fourth, what kind of answer. Not a speech. Not polished. Whatever the word stirred up. Thanks, if it was comfort. Sorrow, if it showed you something wrong. A request, if it showed you a need. Even a complaint: the psalms are full of people arguing with God, and the Church prays them every day. Remember the father in Mark who cried help my unbelief? One sentence, with tears. That counts. The Catechism describes prayer as a living relationship, God's thirst meeting ours. Lectio divina just gives the relationship something to talk about.
screen: `ORATIO: SPEECH, FROM THE MOUTH.` · `FROM THE WORD TO THE ONE WHO SPOKE.` · `SPEAK, LORD, SAMUEL ANSWERS.` · `THANKS, SORROW, ASKING, COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak one honest sentence back. Settle and breathe. Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Go back to your word, and what it stirred up over the last two days. Now answer. One honest sentence, quietly or inside. If you pray, say it to God, as simply as you'd say it to a friend. If you don't, say it to the words themselves, or to the quiet. Then let the sentence sit there. The bell holds the time.
Oratio. Latin for prayer and for speech: the third rung, answering back to God with whatever the word stirred up. Today's word.
Your line: answer back. Today, reply to one message you've been leaving unanswered, and make the reply honest. Day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Lectio divina, 4: rest
236.hook: stop talking and rest in what's been given
236.howItsDone: Catholics who practice lectio divina usually end it with a few minutes of silence, simply resting in God's presence, and many monasteries and parishes keep times of silent prayer after the readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oratio, the third rung: you answered the word with one honest sentence. Your line was answer back. What did you say? Today, the top of the ladder, where you stop talking. Day two hundred thirty-six.

Think of the end of a long talk with an old friend, late at night. You've said everything that needed saying. Nobody reaches for their phone. Nobody fills the quiet. You just sit there together, and it's the best part of the evening. Couples who've been married fifty years know this silence. So do grandparents holding a sleeping baby. The monks said lectio divina ends there too. After reading, chewing and answering, the fourth rung isn't another thing to do. It's the moment you stop doing.
screen: `THE END OF A LONG TALK.` → `NOBODY FILLS THE QUIET.` → `THE FOURTH RUNG: STOP DOING.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Contemplatio, Latin for contemplation. We met it four days ago, with the farmer at Ars: I look at him, he looks at me. Now you can see where it sits: at the top of Guigo's ladder. Reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes. It's the only rung you can't climb by trying. Guigo says that while the soul is still asking, God interrupts the prayer, and comes to meet it. Second, a gift, not an achievement. The Catholic tradition is clear on this: you can't make contemplation happen. You can only make room. Read, chew, answer, and then be quiet and let God do what God does. Some days that silence is full. Some days it's just quiet, and that's fine too. Third, the model. Luke tells of two sisters, Martha and Mary, welcoming Jesus. Martha is busy serving. Mary sits at his feet, listening. When Martha complains, Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." The Church has never said serving is bad; Martha is a saint too. But there's a time to sit. Fourth, back to our verse, and its last promise: I will refresh you. In Greek, the word means I will give you rest. That's the top of the ladder. You came burdened. You read, you chewed, you answered. Now you rest. Back in camp four we met the psalm of the weaned child, quiet against its mother. The monks said contemplation is like that. Not asleep. Just close, and still.
screen: `CONTEMPLATIO: THE TOP RUNG.` · `A GIFT, NOT AN ACHIEVEMENT.` · `MARY HATH CHOSEN THE BEST PART.` · `I WILL GIVE YOU REST.` · then, large: `BUT ONE THING IS NECESSARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit wordless for two minutes. Say the verse one last time: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Then stop. No more words. Don't chew, don't answer, don't plan. Just sit, the way you'd sit with an old friend at the end of the night. If thoughts come, let them pass like cars on a far-off road. If you pray, simply rest in God's company. If you don't, rest in the quiet itself. The bell holds the time.
Contemplatio. The fourth rung: after reading, chewing and answering, you stop, and rest in what's been given. Today's word.
Your line: rest in it. Today, after something good, a meal, a conversation, a finished task, don't rush to the next thing. Stay one minute longer. Day two hundred thirty-six.

237.title: The examen
237.hook: Ignatius's daily look back: thanks, light, review, sorrow, hope
237.howItsDone: Many Catholics, especially those formed by the Jesuits, pray the examen once or twice a day, often at night, and an examination of conscience is also how Catholics prepare for confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the top of the ladder: contemplatio, stop talking and rest. Your line was rest in it. Where did you stay one minute longer? Lectio divina reads a page of Scripture. Today, a way to read the page of your own day. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

In 1521, a young Basque soldier named Iñigo was defending the fortress of Pamplona when a cannonball smashed his leg. Months in bed, bored out of his mind, he asked for adventure novels. The house only had a life of Christ and a book of saints. He read them, and noticed something odd: daydreams of glory left him empty afterward, and daydreams of following Christ left him glad. He'd started paying attention to what was happening inside him. That soldier became Saint Ignatius of Loyola. And the habit became today's word.
screen: `1521: A CANNONBALL AT PAMPLONA.` → `ONLY TWO BOOKS IN THE HOUSE.` → `HE STARTS PAYING ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Examen is Latin, and it has a lovely old meaning: the needle on a balance scale, the little pointer that shows which way things tip. An examen is a daily look at which way your day tipped. Second, the steps. In his Spiritual Exercises, published in 1548, Ignatius lays out a short daily prayer in five points. Today it's often summed up in five words: thanks, light, review, sorrow, hope. Thanks: begin by remembering what you were given today. Light: ask God for the grace to see your day clearly and honestly. Review: walk back through the day, hour by hour, like watching a film. Where was there life? Where did you go wrong? Sorrow: ask forgiveness for what needs it. Hope: look toward tomorrow, and ask for help with it. Third, the order. Notice what comes first. Not your sins. Thanks. Ignatius puts gratitude before examining anything, and many who teach the examen say that's the secret: you look at your day as someone who has been loved all day long. It's not an audit. It's a conversation about the day with someone who was there. Fourth, why it lasts. Ignatius founded the Jesuits, and the story is often told that he let his companions shorten other prayers when they were busy or sick, but never the examen. Today it's prayed in Jesuit schools, in homes at bedtime, even by people who've never met a Jesuit. It takes ten or fifteen minutes. The question at its heart is the one in your line: where was God today?
screen: `EXAMEN: THE NEEDLE ON A SCALE.` · `THANKS, LIGHT, REVIEW, SORROW, HOPE.` · `GRATITUDE COMES FIRST.` · `NEVER SKIP THE EXAMEN.` · then, large: `WHERE WAS GOD TODAY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short examen now, and a full one tonight. Settle and breathe. Thanks: name one thing from today you're grateful for. Light: ask to see honestly. Review: run back through today so far, like a film on fast forward. Stop where you felt most alive. Stop where you felt worst. Sorrow: if something needs forgiving, name it. Hope: think of the rest of today. If you pray, do all five with God. If you don't, do them with honest attention. Tonight, before sleep, try it again, slower. The bell holds the time.
Examen. Latin for the needle on a scale: Saint Ignatius's daily five-step look back at the day, beginning with thanks. Today's word.
Your line: where was god today. Tonight, before you fall asleep, ask that question once, and answer it with one moment. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

238.title: Consolation and desolation
238.hook: what draws you toward God and what drags you away
238.howItsDone: Catholics who make Ignatian retreats or meet with a spiritual director often talk through their consolations and desolations, using Ignatius's rules for the discernment of spirits to make decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's five steps, beginning with thanks. Your line was where was god today. What moment did you find? Today, the two words Ignatius used for what you find when you look. And the week ends. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

Some evenings you come home and you feel light. You were kind to someone, or someone was kind to you, and the world seems roomy. Other evenings you come home heavy. Everything's gray, you snap at people, and the idea of praying, or trying at all, feels pointless. Most of us just call these good days and bad days. Ignatius of Loyola, lying in that bed with his broken leg, noticed they were more than moods. They were movements, pulling him in two directions. He gave them names, and those names are still used by spiritual directors today.
screen: `SOME EVENINGS YOU FEEL LIGHT.` → `SOME EVENINGS, EVERYTHING'S GRAY.` → `NOT MOODS: MOVEMENTS.`

segments.voice: First, consolation. From the Latin for comfort, being comforted. In his Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius describes consolation as any inner movement that draws the soul toward God: an increase of faith, hope and love, a deep peace, joy that lifts you toward what matters. Second, desolation. The opposite pull. Darkness, restlessness, a drift toward low things, feeling lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise: consolation isn't the same as feeling good. Tears of sorrow for something you've done wrong can be consolation, because they turn you toward God. And a fun, busy week can hide desolation, if it's quietly pulling you away. The question isn't how do I feel. It's which way am I being pulled. Third, the rules. Ignatius gives advice for both. The most famous: in desolation, never make a change. Don't quit, don't break up, don't move across the country when everything feels dark. Stay with the decisions you made in a better light, pray a little more, and wait. Desolation passes. And in consolation, enjoy it, give thanks, and store up strength for the harder days. Fourth, what this means. Catholics don't read desolation as proof God has left. Ignatius says God can allow it, to teach us that consolation is a gift, not something we manufacture. The whole practice is simply noticing the pull. This week in camp five: contemplation, then the four rungs of lectio divina, read, meditate, pray, rest, then the examen, and now consolation. Every one of them is a way of paying attention.
screen: `CONSOLATION: DRAWN TOWARD GOD.` · `DESOLATION: DRAGGED AWAY.` · `IN DESOLATION, MAKE NO CHANGE.` · `A GIFT, NOT MANUFACTURED.` · then, large: `WHICH WAY AM I BEING PULLED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name today's high and low. Settle and breathe. Go back over the last day. Find the moment you felt most drawn toward life, toward love, toward God if you believe. Name it in a few words. That's your consolation. Now find the moment you felt most pulled away, dragged down, closed in. Name it too, without judging it. That's your desolation. Notice the direction of each, not just the feeling. If you pray, bring both to God, the high with thanks, the low with honesty. The bell holds the time.
Consolation. In Ignatius's language, any movement that draws you toward God, even through tears. Its opposite is desolation. Today's word.
Your line: notice the pull. Today, if a heavy mood tempts you to make a big decision, wait. Make it on a lighter day. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

myth: consolation just means feeling good
it's any movement toward God, even tears of sorrow. a fun week can hide desolation.
Ignatius advises never to make a change in desolation
stay with decisions made in a better light, pray, and wait.
Ignatius says desolation proves God has left you
he says God can allow it, to teach that consolation is a gift.

fork.setup: you're in a gray, heavy stretch. praying feels pointless, and you're tempted to quit something you chose carefully a year ago. what does Ignatius advise?
options: quit now, while you're clear-eyed.
make no change; stay with what you decided in a better light.
stop praying until the mood lifts.
fork.reveal: in desolation, never make a change. stay firm, pray a little more, and wait. desolation passes.

original.note: Latin: comfort, consolation. from con-, with, and solari, to comfort.

trapdoor: what you thought: good days and bad days.
what it means: movements toward God and away from God, noticed by their direction, not just their feeling.
what a scholar hears: Ignatius's rules for the discernment of spirits (Exercises 313–336), especially 316–318 on consolation, desolation, and no change.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, nos. 313–336 (rules for the discernment of spirits), esp. 316–318, 322
